title: Struck silent (Luke 1:18–25)
hookLine: he doubts and can't speak for nine months; Elizabeth hides and rejoices

lines: THE NEWS HE HAD PRAYED FOR.
cards: An angel has just promised Zechariah the son he and Elisabeth prayed for. And what does he say? Not thank you.
Not finally. In the King James Bible: "Whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man, and my wife well stricken in years." How can I be sure?
It's such a human reply. After that long, hope can feel dangerous. Good news arrives, and the first move is to look for the catch.
But this messenger is not amused. He tells Zechariah exactly who he is.

teach.b: "I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God; and am sent to speak unto thee, and to shew thee these glad tidings."

Then the sign Zechariah asked for, though not the one he wanted: "thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed." Dumb, in older English, means unable to speak.

Outside, the crowd wonders why he's taking so long. When he comes out, he can't say a word, only make signs with his hands. Near the end of Luke's Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his friends.
Some readers see the Gospel opening with a blessing that couldn't be spoken, and closing with one that is.

Zechariah goes home in silence, and Elisabeth conceives. She hides herself five months, and says: "Thus hath the Lord dealt with me in the days wherein he looked on me, to take away my reproach among men."
Reproach is her own word for the way people had looked at her. Now the Lord has looked on her. She keeps it close.
So the house is quiet: a man who can't speak, a woman who won't, and a child growing in the silence.

teach.h: THOU SHALT BE DUMB, AND NOT ABLE TO SPEAK.
teach.b: Christians read Zechariah's silence more than one way: as a consequence of doubt, and as a gift, months to listen instead of talk.

This week has come a long way: a mother who can't forget, a balm, a scroll in Nazareth, the prophets' voices, Luke's careful letter, an old priest's prayer, and a quiet house where something is growing.

how: Some Christians keep times of silence as a way of waiting, especially in Advent, and some monastic rules, like Saint Benedict's, make silence part of daily life.

o: Zechariah's own vow to keep quiet in the temple
Zechariah's sign: no voice until the promise came true
Elisabeth's choice to hide her news for five months

games.q: what's inside Luke 1:18–25 — tap the pairs.
p: stands in the presence of God

s: Zechariah thanked the angel right away
he asked how he could be sure: "whereby shall I know this?"
Zechariah came out to the waiting crowd unable to speak
he came out unable to speak and could only make signs.
Elisabeth announced her news to everyone at once
she hid herself five months, saying the Lord had looked on her.

games.q: you're Zechariah. an angel has just promised you a son in your old age. what do you say?
o: how can I be sure? I'm an old man.
games.why: "whereby shall I know this? for I am an old man." Gabriel gives him a sign: silence, until the promise comes true.

practice: Let the silence be as complete as you can; when words start up in your head, notice them and let them pass, like Zechariah's crowd outside the door.
Then think of one place you usually fill with words, a meeting, an explanation, advice nobody asked for, and picture leaving a little more quiet there.
If you pray, offer your silence to God as a kind of listening; if not, simply rest in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Struck silent. Zechariah asks for proof and loses his voice until the promise comes true, while Elisabeth quietly carries the child.

orig.note: Greek: being silent. Gabriel's word for what Zechariah will be until the child comes.

carryVoice: Your line: silence can grow things. Quiet months, and a promise growing. Another week on the path.
